::: {.callout-tip .definition title="Definition"}
A **tokenizer** is the component that turns text into token IDs before a model
sees it, and turns token IDs back into text after the model responds. It is a
fixed vocabulary plus the rules for splitting text against that vocabulary. Both
are set once, then frozen, and every model is trained against one specific
tokenizer.
:::

## More context

The [Token](token.qmd) entry covers what a token is and why models use sub-word
pieces. So what actually produces those pieces? That's the tokenizer, and it's
the focus here. As before, the examples use OpenAI's `o200k_base` tokenizer, the
same one the Token entry uses.

### What a tokenizer holds

Let's start with what's inside one. A tokenizer isn't a neural network. It's a
small bundle of fixed data and rules, with no weights to train, so the same text
always gives you the same IDs. There are four pieces worth knowing:

- **Vocabulary.** A lookup table that pairs every known piece of text with an
  integer ID. `o200k_base` has roughly 200,000 entries.
- **Splitting rules.** The instructions for breaking text into pieces that exist
  in the vocabulary. In `o200k_base` they run in two stages. First, a fixed
  pattern cuts the text into chunks. Then an ordered list of BPE merges joins
  pieces inside each chunk, and never across a chunk boundary. One rule in the
  pattern is `\p{N}{1,3}`, meaning "runs of 1 to 3 digits". That's why the Token
  entry shows `12345.67` becoming `123` `45` `.` `67`. The digit grouping comes
  from the splitting rules, not the vocabulary.
- **Special tokens.** Reserved IDs that stand for control markers rather than
  text, such as `<|endoftext|>`. They mark things like where a document or a chat
  message ends.
- **Normalization.** Some tokenizers also clean up text before splitting it, for
  example with Unicode clean-up or lowercasing
  ([Hugging Face pipeline docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/tokenizers/pipeline)).
  tiktoken's encodings skip this step.

Where does all of this come from? The vocabulary and the merges are learned from
a large body of text in a one-time step called tokenizer training. The split
pattern and the special tokens are chosen by the people who design the
tokenizer. Once a model is trained on it, none of the existing entries can
change.

Why does it matter that the same text always gives the same IDs? Two reasons.
First, you can count tokens offline with `tiktoken` and trust that OpenAI's
servers split the same text the same way. Second, when later lessons show a model
giving different answers to the same prompt, even at temperature 0, you'll know
the variation isn't coming from the tokenizer.

### It runs in both directions

Here's something that's easy to miss: a tokenizer sits on both sides of the
model. Your prompt goes in through it, and the model's reply comes back out
through it. The model itself only ever handles IDs.

| Direction | Input | Output | When it runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Encode | Text | Token IDs | Before the model, on your prompt |
| Decode | Token IDs | Text | After the model, on each ID it generates |

Notice that the round trip is lossless. Decode the IDs and you get back exactly
the text you encoded ([tiktoken README](https://github.com/openai/tiktoken)).
That's why the same tokenizer can both prepare your prompt and render the model's
reply.

### Why a tokenizer is tied to a model

Could you swap GPT-4o's tokenizer for an entirely different one? Not without
retraining the model. Here's the reason: during training, the model learns what
each ID means. If ID 9059 was `" cat"` for the whole of training, then everything
the model has learned about 9059 is "cat-like."

Now hand the same text to a different tokenizer, and you'll get different IDs.
Feed those to the original model and it reads a scrambled message, even though
your text never changed. So the tokenizer is chosen first, the model is trained
on its output, and the two ship as a pair. GPT-4 is paired with `cl100k_base` and
GPT-4o with `o200k_base`, which is why token counts differ between them.

Adding to a tokenizer is a different story. Teams often add special tokens when
they fine-tune, for example. The model then needs new embedding rows for those
tokens, and fine-tuning trains them without a full retrain. What breaks a model
is changing or removing tokens it already knows, because their IDs then mean
something different.

### Where BPE fits

These two terms often get used interchangeably, so let's separate them.
"Tokenizer" names the component. Byte pair encoding (BPE) is one method for
building one: it starts from small units and repeatedly merges the most frequent
pair until the vocabulary reaches a target size. WordPiece and Unigram are other
methods that fill the same role. `tiktoken` is OpenAI's BPE tokenizer library.

It helps to keep two phases apart:

1. **Training the tokenizer** happens once and produces the vocabulary and merge
   rules.
2. **Using the tokenizer** happens on every request and only applies those rules.

## Usage example

The Token entry counted tokens. Here, let's watch the tokenizer itself at work.
It only takes a few lines of Python: encode a sentence, look at each piece, and
decode it back.

```python
import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")

text = "The cat sat on the mat!"

ids = enc.encode(text)                    # text -> token IDs
pieces = [enc.decode([i]) for i in ids]   # each ID back to its piece
restored = enc.decode(ids)                # token IDs -> text

print(ids)
print(pieces)
print(restored == text)
```

```text
[976, 9059, 10139, 402, 290, 2450, 0]
['The', ' cat', ' sat', ' on', ' the', ' mat', '!']
True
```

Notice anything? Each line of the script tells you something about how a
tokenizer works:

- `get_encoding` loads the frozen vocabulary and splitting rules. Nothing is
  learned at this point.
- `encode` is the only step the model needs before it runs. The model receives
  the seven integers, not the sentence.
- `decode` is a pure lookup. The leading spaces live inside the pieces, which is
  how the text comes back exactly.
- `True` confirms the round trip is lossless.

## What to avoid

- **Treating the tokenizer as part of the model's intelligence.** It's a
  deterministic lookup with no understanding of meaning. Meaning starts at the
  embedding step.
- **Using "tokenizer" and "BPE" as synonyms.** The tokenizer is the component,
  and BPE is just one way to build it.
- **Assuming one tokenizer per provider.** GPT-4 and GPT-4o use different ones.
  Check the model, not the company.
- **Expecting `encode(text)` to match the API's token count exactly.** Chat
  requests wrap your messages in special tokens, so the billed count runs a little
  higher. Use the provider's token-counting endpoint when the exact number
  matters.
- **Decoding one token at a time and assuming whole characters.** A single token
  can hold part of a multi-byte character, such as an emoji. Decode the full
  sequence, or buffer when streaming.
- **Changing or removing tokens a model already knows.** Their IDs would then mean
  something different from what the model learned, so you'd have to retrain it.
  Adding tokens is fine and common: teams add special tokens when they fine-tune,
  and the model learns new embedding rows for them without a full retrain.

## Related terms

- **[Token](token.qmd):** one piece of text the tokenizer produces; the unit
  models read, write, and bill in.
- **Token ID:** the integer the tokenizer assigns to a token. The model only ever
  sees these.
- **Vocabulary:** the fixed table of every token a tokenizer knows, with its ID.
- **Byte pair encoding (BPE):** a common algorithm for building a tokenizer by
  merging frequent pairs.
- **Special token:** a reserved ID for a control marker, such as end of text,
  rather than for text itself.
- **Embedding:** the vector a model looks up for each token ID; the reason a model
  and its tokenizer can't be separated.
- **Encode and decode:** the two directions a tokenizer runs, text to IDs and IDs
  to text.
